name: Dana Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Your answers are confidential, including anything you tell me privately. What does a normal workday hold for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead six people who track possible faults in household appliances for a large manufacturer. We read repair reports, spot a pattern and decide which cases need a safety review; then I bring engineers, service centres and customer staff into the same room. I use an AI tool every day to sort the first pile of reports, but I still open the originals because one odd sentence can matter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you proud of in that work, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We caught a batch of kettles with cracked handles before anyone got badly burned, and I was proud my team kept asking for photos. The hard part is telling someone their appliance is safe when I haven't finished checking it. I'm 27, have an MBA and live with my partner Malik, who photographs events; his bookings jump around. I have about four months of expenses saved, and my pay is decent but ordinary for this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daily sorting tool might remain a time saver, and the safety reviews would still land with us. That's a workable future. Malik's event bookings were patchy this autumn, though, so a quiet AI story wouldn't make our household feel rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep using the report sorter for first passes, then check every serious case against photos. I'd tell friends AI saved us some dull reading, not the decision about whether a kettle goes back on sale. I wouldn't promise it could spot every fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I like this picture. I could keep a job I'm good at and perhaps move up when our director retires. But four months of expenses is not much when Malik can have an empty calendar after a busy season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next month I'd keep our weekly photo review and write down the few mistakes the sorter makes. Through the first year of a plateau I'd stay with the team and move 200 a month from takeaways into our emergency account, provided Malik's bookings cover his share of rent. If his bookings don't, I'd cut the transfer before borrowing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled about work. A dry month for Malik still makes me watch the account balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the sorter miss most recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repair report said 'warm at the seam', and the tool filed it as a normal heat complaint. We opened the photo and saw the handle split where a child would grip it. That's why I won't throw away the originals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident at work. Why keep building cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Malik had two weddings cancelled in October and the rent didn't care. We covered it without debt, but I watched the balance fall. A small transfer each month buys us fewer worried Sundays.

say: The sorter saves **reading time**, while my team still checks serious repair photos.
A machine's first pass cannot make the **safety release** decision on its own.
think: My **role stays useful**, and I could seek the director's post later.
Four months saved feels thin when **Malik's bookings** fall for a season.
do: Keep the **weekly photo review** and record sorter mistakes.
Move **200 a month** from takeaways to cash if Malik covers his rent share.
feel: I feel **settled** at work, with some worry about the household balance.
S0.quote: A small transfer each month buys us fewer worried Sundays.
fieldNote: She trusts the tool for **sorting**, but the cracked handle case keeps her checking source photos.
Her **four-month reserve** gives room, though Malik's variable bookings still weigh on her.
The monthly saving is **conditional** on their rent being covered first.

steps.text: Keep the weekly photo review and record missed faults in repair reports
Transfer 200 monthly from takeaways if Malik covers his rent share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and checking are exactly where my six people spend their mornings. A stronger system could rank fault reports, draft customer replies and schedule service visits while robots are still nowhere near a workbench. I could run that change, but I won't assume it needs six analysts afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we'll measure what the software gets right and wrong before any new targets are set. To friends I'd say some office posts will shrink, even if repair shops still need people. I'd speak up if a safety check is being sold as a clerical step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be kept as the manager who signs a decision, or I might be one of several managers competing for one post. I enjoy new tools and I could lead a pilot, but a clever pilot could erase jobs I recruited people into. I don't know which way the company would price that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd propose a three-month pilot on closed repair cases and have two analysts score the tool's missed safety warnings. I'd learn the new audit settings alongside them rather than asking them to carry it alone. In the first year of rollout, if our director approves it, I'd automate only the report sorting and ask to keep a named human review before any safety release; I'd also check two nearby employers' posted safety roles, without resigning for an advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested and uneasy together. The people I trained are not a spare line on my spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two people would score the pilot, and are they willing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Priya, who notices strange repair language, and Leon, who knows service centre photos. They would be paid on our normal hours, not asked to do a second shift for my experiment. If either says no, I'd choose another reviewer instead of dressing it up as voluntary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot misses a dangerous case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop that part of the rollout and show the original report to engineering. A saved hour doesn't cover a burned hand. I would rather explain a delay than sign a release I can't defend.

say: Measure **missed safety warnings** before raising targets or reducing reviews.
Repair shops still need hands, but **office posts** could shrink.
think: I could lead the pilot and still **lose my post** to a smaller management team.
Automating work done by people I recruited leaves me **uneasy**.
do: Run a **three-month closed-case pilot** with paid analyst review if approved.
Learn the tool's **audit settings** with the two reviewers.
Check **two nearby safety vacancies** without leaving a paid job.
feel: I feel **interested**, and uneasy about the team's jobs and my own.
S1.quote: A saved hour doesn't cover a burned hand.
fieldNote: She separates **report sorting** from the human safety release and physical repair work.
Her proposed pilot includes **paid review time** and a stop point for missed warnings.
She sees a path to lead change but cannot assume **management posts** stay numerous.

steps.text: Learn the new audit settings with two analysts during paid review time
Pilot automatic report sorting on closed cases if the director approves
Check posted safety roles at two nearby employers without resigning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a system that can reason better than us can read the fault report, weigh the photo and write the release advice. My safety sign-off might remain for legal reasons, but that could be one post for several teams. Service staff still have to open machines until robots arrive around 2031; I don't know how many people would get those posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team honestly that the desk work could change by 2028 and ask for a dated staffing plan. I'd tell Malik we should count his on-site photography separately from the editing software can do. In public I wouldn't call a signature a guaranteed job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my post is likely to go or be cut sharply, and Malik could lose editing fees at the same time. Four months of savings gives us a bridge, not a new career. I'm quick with tools, but that speed may not be worth a salary if AGI does the whole analysis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month we'd cancel the holiday before paying its deposit and put 300 a month into cash while both incomes hold. I'd ask service operations about a paid appliance inspection trainee post, with the wage and vacancy in writing before I apply. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I'd apply for that funded post if it still exists; otherwise I'd use the four-month reserve for a search across the nearby employers, and Malik would keep taking on-site shoots while they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed. The calendar moves faster than a real training place opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection instead of another office management job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to see a failed part in my hands, not only its photograph. Those physical checks could still need people until around 2031, although the reports and scheduling would change in 2028. I wouldn't pay for a course unless a shop would take me on afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the trainee wage is lower, can you afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it covers my share of rent and loan payments; I won't make Malik carry both. We'd put the numbers on the kitchen table before I accept. If the wage fails that test, I'd keep applying for paid work rather than calling the course a solution.

say: The **desk decisions** could change by 2028; a legal signature does not guarantee a post.
Malik's **on-site shoots** may differ from editing work, but neither income is certain.
think: My **post could go**, while Malik loses editing fees at the same time.
Four months of cash is a **bridge**, not enough to fund an unfunded course.
do: Cancel the **holiday** before its deposit and save 300 monthly while both incomes hold.
Ask for a **paid inspection trainee vacancy** with written wages and an opening.
Apply after 2028 only if the **wage** covers rent and loans.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by two exposed incomes and a short training window.
S2.quote: Four months of savings gives us a bridge, not a new career.
fieldNote: She expects **desk exposure in 2028** and distinguishes it from physical inspections until robots arrive around 2031.
Her trainee plan requires **an actual funded vacancy** and wages that cover her bills.
The household also faces **Malik's editing income** shrinking, so four months saved feels brief.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday before paying its deposit now
Save 300 monthly while both household incomes hold
Apply for a paid inspection trainee post if its wage covers her bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me learn what a service inspection actually involves instead of running toward the first open door. The analysis and release advice could still be automated by 2031; hands-on checks would face capable robots around 2034. The extra time matters, but it's not a promise that the shop will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team there is time to train on the company's clock if posts are real. To Malik I'd say we can plan a move only after seeing what both our incomes look like. I wouldn't tell anyone that five years makes the safety desk safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move into field quality work, where someone opens returned machines and checks the failed part, if there is an opening. It's still risky because its paperwork changes in 2031 and robots could take the bench work around 2034. At least I might save enough to refuse a bad offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd ask for one paid inspection day each month with the service centre, and if they agree I'd complete those days and learn the tests on real returned kettles. I'd add 250 a month to savings while Malik's bookings cover his share of rent, aiming for six months of expenses by 2030. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted field quality role only if its pay covers our bills; otherwise I'd search the other service centres with my cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but I can make several choices instead of one rushed guess. Five years lets me find out whether I even like the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a paid inspection day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open a returned kettle with the technician, photograph the cracked handle and trace the batch number back to the repair report. The technician makes the electrical checks; I'd need proper instruction before doing that myself. That day would tell me whether my desk judgment helps at the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Suppose the service centre says no to those days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my paid role and ask another nearby centre about a supervised visit. I wouldn't call myself trained after watching a video. If no one can offer real practice, I'd prepare for other management vacancies too.

say: Five years can fund **real inspection practice** if the employer offers paid time.
The **safety desk** is still exposed when AGI arrives in 2031.
think: Field quality might suit me, but **paperwork changes** in 2031 and bench work later.
A bigger reserve would let me **refuse low pay** rather than grab any post.
do: Complete **monthly paid inspection days** next spring if the service centre agrees.
Save **250 monthly** toward six months of expenses if Malik covers his rent share.
Apply for a **posted field quality role** after 2031 only at affordable pay.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough time to test a real option.
S3.quote: I wouldn't call myself trained after watching a video.
fieldNote: She seeks **supervised bench practice**, while recognising electrical checks need instruction.
The plan keeps **2031 paperwork exposure** separate from possible robot work around 2034.
Savings and a move depend on **both incomes**, real openings and affordable pay.

steps.text: Complete monthly supervised kettle inspections on paid time if approved
Save 250 monthly if Malik’s bookings cover his share of rent
Apply for a posted field quality job after 2031 only if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for me to stay in safety work and also build another way to earn. By 2036 the software might do most analysis and release advice; physical inspection may still need hands until roughly 2039. I would have to see whether customers still pay for a person to look at a returned appliance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should pay for people to learn the hands-on checks before it cuts desk posts. I'd also say there is time to build a savings buffer instead of telling everyone to take a leap. To friends I'd admit I want more than one pay source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use the decade to become the person who connects a customer's complaint to the thing on the bench. I don't know whether the firm would keep that combined role by 2036, so I'd rather have a modest second income. Malik's event work might change too, and I don't want to make our rent depend on one clever plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the service director for two paid bench afternoons a month, and if approved I'd do them alongside a technician to learn the safe checks. After I have that experience and written permission from the company to work outside hours, I'd offer weekend appliance check-ups if a local repair shop agrees to host me for a fee, starting with one Saturday a month and no electrical repairs beyond my training. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd keep that shop work only if it still has paying customers and meets the shop's safety rules, using our saved cushion if my office post ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, with a little edge to it. Ten years feels workable, though not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the company let you work at a repair shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I'd ask in writing before I took a fee. They may see it as a conflict even if I avoid our products. If they refuse, I can still learn on their paid time and keep the money in savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Malik think about Saturdays at the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He shoots most weekends, so we'd need to choose dates when neither of us is booked. I'd tell him I want one paid test day before committing to a regular Saturday. My partner's event shoots and my repair shifts could turn every Saturday into two separate workdays.

say: Pay for **hands-on training** before removing desk posts.
A decade allows **savings and second income** if the rules and customers permit.
think: A combined bench and complaint role may **not last** through 2036.
One modest **second income** could soften a loss of either household wage.
do: Complete **two paid bench afternoons** monthly if the director approves.
Offer **one Saturday check-up** monthly only if a shop hosts me and my employer agrees.
Keep weekend work after 2036 only if **customers pay** and safety rules allow.
feel: I feel **curious**, with uncertainty about the role and the shop work.
S4.quote: My partner's event shoots and my repair shifts could turn every Saturday into two separate workdays.
fieldNote: Her side work depends on **written employer permission**, technician training and a repair shop willing to host her.
She keeps the **2036 desk change** separate from physical work exposed around 2039.
Malik's weekend shoots affect whether **Saturday work** is practical.

steps.text: Complete two paid bench afternoons monthly if the service director approves
Offer paid check-ups within training limits only after training, employer permission and shop agreement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The software could take the report reading and the decisions before I have time to move into a role where I touch the faulty product, and Malik's editing income could fall too. A clear date for any cuts, a paid place on a service training course and access to real openings would help; I wouldn't count a brochure as an opening.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who keeps the photo when the software calls a kettle safe? An injured customer will need to know which report was checked and who had authority to release the batch. I want that record whatever happens to my own job.

headlineQuote: An injured customer will need to know which report was checked and who had authority to release the batch.
portrait: Dana, **27**, leads six appliance fault analysts at a large manufacturer and uses AI daily to sort repair reports.
Her **MBA and strong record** help her lead safety reviews, but her pay is typical and she has four months saved.
Her partner's **event photography** brings uneven income, so fast changes could squeeze both sides of their household budget.
She would pursue **paid service training** and physical inspections if a real opening exists, while keeping a record of safety decisions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her desk role while Malik's photo editing work also loses income.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear cut date** and access to actual service openings before her wages stop.
A **paid training place** for hands-on appliance inspection if the company funds one.
